one_liner: Header-only C++17 work-stealing thread pool with recursion-safe futures; beats std::async on small and recursive tasks.
what_it_does: utl::parallel is one module of a header-only C++17 utility collection, providing tasks, parallel-for loops, and parallel reductions via a Scheduler/ThreadPool API similar in spirit to Intel TBB. It targets the specific failure mode where naive std::async/std::thread per-task creation overhead cripples small-task throughput, and where scatter-gather workloads with awaited nested subtasks deadlock most existing thread pools. It is not a drop-in std::async replacement: task submission uses detached_task/awaitable_task/blocking_loop-style calls, and awaitable_task returns a custom future_type rather than std::future.
how_it_is_fast: Work-stealing thread pool: each worker has a local LIFO deque fed by recursively spawned tasks (kept hot in cache) plus a global FIFO queue for externally submitted tasks; idle threads steal from the back of other workers' local deques. Recursive awaiting is made safe by a custom future_type wrapping std::future whose get()/wait() search for stealable work locally instead of blocking outright, which is what avoids both the thread-creation overhead of std::async and the deadlocks that plain std::future-based pools hit on nested awaits.
when_to_use: Many small (well under 1ms) tasks where std::async's per-call thread-spawn overhead dominates runtime
Recursive/scatter-gather workloads (divide-and-conquer, fan-out fibonacci-style spawning) that need awaitable subtasks without deadlocking
Header-only C++17 codebases that want a single dependency-free, vendorable (~600-900 LOC) thread pool instead of pulling in a framework
Cross-platform targets (Windows, Linux, macOS, FreeBSD all CI-tested) needing a pool with no platform-specific code
Parallel-for / parallel-reduce over containers or index ranges with automatic grain-size splitting
when_not_to_use: Large uniform non-recursive tasks (1-3ms+): advantage over std::async nearly vanishes (~1.06x, roughly tied)
Workloads wanting a vendor-optimized scheduler (OpenMP/TBB-class NUMA-aware or SIMD-tuned scheduling) — author explicitly disclaims superiority over those
Code that needs a real std::future everywhere (generic code pattern-matching on std::future<T>); future_type is a custom wrapper, only constructible from std::future, not one itself
Projects already committed to a C++20-only recursive pool (Leopard, riften::ThiefPool) if that ecosystem fits better; utl::parallel is intentionally capped at C++17

High-stakes throughput decisions without your own validation: this is the project's single-machine (consumer laptop) benchmark with no independent third-party reproduction, and the library is small (336 stars) and young

integration.platforms: any (CI-tested on Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, FreeBSD); no platform-specific code
integration.thread_safety: All ThreadPool methods (including set_thread_count, task submission) are thread-safe and callable concurrently from any number of external threads. Calling set_thread_count() from a thread that is itself inside the pool throws std::runtime_error instead of deadlocking.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: task submission API (detached_task/awaitable_task/blocking_loop) differs from std::async(), and awaitable_task returns a custom future_type (constructible from std::future, same method surface) rather than std::future itself, which is required specifically so recursive get()/wait() can steal work instead of deadlocking.

gotchas: future_type is not std::future; code that specifically requires std::future<T> (e.g. via type traits) won't accept it directly, only convert from one
set_thread_count() blocks until all in-flight tasks finish before resizing, and throws std::runtime_error if invoked from inside the pool on itself
Default grain size is hardware_concurrency()*4 subranges; very unevenly-costed per-element work may need a manually tuned grain_size
Only 4 of the module's benchmark scenarios include BS::thread_pool/progschj/ThreadPool as recursion baselines; those two deadlock outright once tasks await nested subtasks
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick utl::parallel over BS::thread_pool or meet1214/thread-pool when the workload has recursively-awaited subtasks — both siblings deadlock on that pattern per UTL's own benchmark, while utl::parallel stays correct and ~3.6x faster than std::async. For large-scale or NUMA-sensitive scatter-gather work, the oneTBB-class siblings (Taskflow, dispenso, TooManyCooks, libfork) are the more feature-complete choice; utl::parallel wins when you want a minimal, dependency-free, copy-pastable single header instead of a full framework.
verified_claims_summary: On a 6-core AMD Ryzen 5 5600H (hyper-threading off), g++ 11.4.0 -O2, against libstdc++: utl::parallel::ThreadPool reached 573.3% of serial throughput vs std::async's 214.0% on small (0-100us) tasks (~2.7x faster) and 583.0%/565.1% vs 161.1%/154.7% on shallow/deep recursive tasks (~3.6x faster), where BS::thread_pool and progschj/ThreadPool deadlocked entirely; on large (1-3ms) tasks the two were nearly tied (597.0% vs 564.2%, ~1.06x).
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2025-12-08 on master; 336 stars); MIT-licensed, header-only, small enough (~600-900 LOC for this module) to vendor directly into a project.
